source_text: Καὶ διὰ τοῦτο χάριν ἔλαβον οἱ ἄνθρωποι τὸ καλεῖσθαι θεοὶ καὶ υἱοὶ Θεοῦ. Πρῶτον οὖν τὸ ἴδιον σῶμα ἤγειρεν ὁ Κύριος ἐκ νεκρῶν, καὶ ὕψωσεν ἐν ἑαυτῷ· μετὰ ταῦτα ἐγερεῖ καὶ τὰ μέλη τοῦ σώματος αὐτοῦ, ἵνα χαρίσηται αὐτοῖς τὰ πάντα, ὡς Θεὸς, ὅσα αὐτὸς ὡς ἄνθρωπος ἔλαβεν. Αὐτὸς οὖν ἑαυτῷ χαρίζεται ζωὴν, καὶ αὐτὸς ἑαυτὸν ἁγιάζει, καὶ αὐτὸς ἑαυτὸν ὑψοῖ. Ὅτε οὖν λέγει, ὅτι ὁ Πατὴρ ἡγίασεν αὐτὸν, καὶ ἤγειρεν αὐτὸν, καὶ ἐχαρίσατο αὐτῷ ὄνομα τὸ ὑπὲρ πᾶν ὄνομα, καὶ ἔδωκεν αὐτῷ ζωήν· δῆλον, ὅτι δι' αὐτοῦ τὰ πάντα ποιεῖ ὁ Πατήρ. Δι' αὐτοῦ οὖν αὐτὸν ἐγείρει, καὶ δι' αὐτοῦ αὐτὸν ἁγιάζει, καὶ δι' αὐτοῦ αὐτὸν ὑψοῖ, καὶ δι' αὐτοῦ αὐτῷ ζωὴν δίδωσι. Καὶ ὅτε παρατίθεται τὸ πνεῦμα αὐτοῦ εἰς χεῖρας τοῦ Πατρὸς, ὡς ἄνθρωπος ἑαυτὸν παρατίθεται τῷ Θεῷ, ἵνα πάντας ἀνθρώπους παραθῆται τῷ Θεῷ. Αὐτὸς γάρ ἐστιν ἡ χεὶρ, καὶ αἱ χεῖρες τοῦ Πατρός. Καὶ ὅτε λέγει· Πρὸ δὲ πάντων τῶν βουνῶν γεννᾷ με, ἐκ προσώπου τῆς Ἐκκλησίας λέγει, ἥτις, πρότερον κτισθεῖσα, μετὰ ταῦτα γεννᾶται ἐκ Θεοῦ. Διὰ τοῦτο πρῶτον κεῖται ἐν τῇ Παροι 1005 μίᾳ τὸ, Ἔκτισέ με ὁ Κύριος, καὶ ὕστερος τὸ, ἐγέννησε. Καὶ ὅτε λέγει ἡ Γραφὴ περὶ Πατρός· Οὐχὶ Θεὸς εἷς ἔκτισεν ἡμᾶς; ὁμοίως καὶ περὶ Υἱοῦ λέγει, ὅτι δι' αὐτοῦ ἐκτίσθη τὰ πάντα· τὰ δὲ αὐτὰ καὶ περὶ τοῦ ἁγίου Πνεύματος λέγεται· Ἀντανελεῖς, φησὶ, τὸ πνεῦμα αὐτῶν, καὶ ἐκλείψουσι, καὶ εἰς τὸν χοῦν αὐτῶν ἐπιστρέψουσιν. Ἐξαποστελεῖς τὸ Πνεῦμά σου, καὶ κτισθήσονται, καὶ ἀνακαινιεῖς τὸ πρόσωπον τῆς γῆς. Καὶ ὅτε λέγει ὁ Υἱὸς περὶ Πατρὸς τῷ Πέτρῳ· Μακάριος εἶ, ὅτι σὰρξ καὶ αἷμα οὐκ ἀπεκάλυψέ σοι, ἀλλ' ὁ Πατήρ μου ὁ ἐν τοῖς οὐρανοῖς· τὰ αὐτὰ περὶ ἑαυτοῦ λέγει· Οὐδεὶς ἐπιγινώσκει τὸν Πατέρα εἰ μὴ ὁ Υἱὸς, καὶ ᾧ ἂν βούληται ὁ Υἱὸς ἀποκαλύψαι. Ὁμοίως δὲ καὶ περὶ τοῦ ἁγίου Πνεύματος ὁ Παῦλος λέγει· Ἡμῖν δὲ ἀπεκάλυψεν ὁ Θεὸς διὰ τοῦ Πνεύματος αὐτοῦ. Τὸ γὰρ Πνεῦμα πάντα ἐρευνᾷ, καὶ τὰ βάθη τοῦ Θεοῦ· τίς γὰρ οἶδεν ἀνθρώπων τὰ τοῦ ἀνθρώπου εἰ μὴ τὸ πνεῦμα τοῦ ἀνθρώπου τὸ ἐν αὐτῷ, Οὕτω καὶ τὰ τοῦ Θεοῦ οὐδεὶς ἔγνωκεν εἰ μὴ τὸ Πνεῦμα τοῦ Θεοῦ. Ὥσπερ οὖν τὸ πνεῦμα τοῦ ἀνθρώπου τῆς ἀνθρωπότητος αὐτοῦ καὶ τῆς οὐσίας οὐ κεχώρισται, οὕτω καὶ τὸ Πνεῦμα τοῦ Θεοῦ τῆς θεότητος αὐτοῦ καὶ τῆς οὐσίας οὐκ ἔστιν ἀλλότριον. Καὶ ὅταν λέγῃ ὁ Κύριος ἐν Ἡσαΐᾳ· Υἱοὺς ἐγέννησα καὶ ὕψωσα· αὐτοὶ δέ με ἠθέτησαν, ἐν τῷ Εὐαγγελίῳ λέγει· Τὸ γεγεννημένον ἐκ τῆς σαρκὸς σάρξ ἐστι, καὶ τὸ γεγεννημένον ἐκ τοῦ Πνεύματος πνεῦμά ἐστι. Καὶ πάλιν· Τὸ Πνεῦμα ὅπου θέλει, πνεῖ, καὶ τὴν φωνὴν αὐτοῦ ἀκούεις· ἀλλ' οὐκ οἶδας, πόθεν ἔρχεται, καὶ ποῦ ὑπάγει. Οὕτως ἐστὶ πᾶς ὁ γεγεννημένος ἐκ τοῦ Πνεύματος. Ἐν δὲ τῇ ἀρχῇ τοῦ Εὐαγγελίου Ἰωάννης λέγει· Ὅσοι δὲ ἔλαβον αὐτὸν, ἔδωκεν αὐτοῖς ἐξουσίαν τέκνα Θεοῦ γενέσθαι, τοῖς πιστεύουσιν εἰς τὸ ὄνομα αὐτοῦ· οἳ οὐκ ἐξ αἱμάτων, οὐδὲ ἐκ θελήματος ἀνδρὸς, οὐδὲ ἐκ θελήματος σαρκὸς, ἀλλ' ἐκ Θεοῦ ἐγεννήθησαν.
thought_title: The Son receives as man what he gives as God
orientation: Marcellus continues his argument that whatever Scripture says the Son received belongs to his assumed humanity, while the same works are done by the Father through the Son and by the Spirit.
pass_a_gloss: And because of this human beings received the grace to be called gods and sons of God. First therefore the Lord raised his own body from the dead, and exalted it in himself; after these things he will also raise the members of his body, in order that he may grant them all things, as God, as many things as he himself as a human being received. He himself therefore grants himself life, and he himself sanctifies himself, and he himself exalts himself. When therefore he says that the Father sanctified him, and raised him, and granted him the name above every name, and gave him life; it is clear that through him the Father does all things. Through him therefore he raises him, and through him he sanctifies him, and through him he exalts him, and through him he gives him life. And when he entrusts his spirit into the hands of the Father, as a human being he entrusts himself to God, in order that he may entrust all human beings to God. For he himself is the hand, and the hands of the Father. And when he says: 'Before all the hills he begets me,' he speaks from the person of the Church, which, having been created first, after these things is begotten from God. Because of this first is placed in the Proverbs the saying, 'The Lord created me,' and later the saying, 'he begot.' And when the Scripture says about the Father: 'Did not one God create us?' likewise also about the Son it says that through him all things were created; and the same things also are said about the Holy Spirit: 'You will take away,' it says, 'their spirit, and they will fail, and to their dust they will return. You will send forth your Spirit, and they will be created, and you will renew the face of the earth.' And when the Son says about the Father to Peter: 'Blessed are you, because flesh and blood did not reveal it to you, but my Father who is in the heavens'; the same things he says about himself: 'No one knows the Father except the Son, and the one to whom the Son chooses to reveal him.' Likewise also about the Holy Spirit Paul says: 'But to us God revealed it through his Spirit. For the Spirit searches all things, even the depths of God; for who among human beings knows the things of a human being except the spirit of the human being that is in him? So also the things of God no one has known except the Spirit of God.' Just as therefore the spirit of a human being is not separated from his humanity and from his substance, so also the Spirit of God is not alien to his deity and to his substance. And when the Lord says in Isaiah: 'Sons I begot and exalted; but they rejected me,' in the Gospel he says: 'That which is born from the flesh is flesh, and that which is born from the Spirit is spirit.' And again: 'The Spirit blows where it wills, and you hear its voice; but you do not know from where it comes, and where it goes. So is everyone who is born from the Spirit.' And in the beginning of the Gospel John says: 'But as many as received him, he gave them authority to become children of God, to those who believe in his name; who were born not from bloods, nor from the will of a man, nor from the will of the flesh, but from God.'

choices.why: Keeps the noun χάρις as 'grace' to preserve the theological sense of a gift from God, not a general favor.
ἴδιον emphasizes the Son's own body as distinct from the members of his body, the Church; 'own' preserves this.
The phrase indicates the exaltation is within the Son's own person, not merely by his power; 'in himself' keeps the reflexive force.

choices.english: from the person of the Church
choices.why: πρόσωπον here means the speaking role or person; 'from the person of' preserves the technical sense of speaking in character.
rejected: in the person of the Church

choices.why: βάθη is plural and means the deep things; 'depths' keeps the plural and the spatial metaphor of the Spirit searching God's innermost reality.
ἀλλότριον means belonging to another, foreign; 'alien' preserves the contrast with being of the same substance.

pass_b_english: And this is why human beings received the grace to be called gods and sons of God. First, then, the Lord raised his own body from the dead and exalted it in himself. After this he will also raise the members of his body, so that as God he may grant them all things—everything that he himself received as a human being. So he grants life to himself, he sanctifies himself, and he exalts himself. When Scripture says that the Father sanctified him, raised him, granted him the name above every name, and gave him life, it is clear that the Father does all things through him. Through him, then, he raises him; through him he sanctifies him; through him he exalts him; and through him he gives him life. And when he entrusts his spirit into the Father's hands, as a human being he entrusts himself to God, so that he may entrust all human beings to God. For he himself is the hand and the hands of the Father. And when he says, "Before all the hills he begets me" (Proverbs 8:25), he speaks from the person of the Church, which was created first and afterward is begotten from God. This is why in Proverbs the words "The Lord created me" (Proverbs 8:22) come first, and "he begot me" comes later. And when Scripture says about the Father, "Did not one God create us?" (Malachi 2:10), it says the same about the Son—that all things were created through him. And the same is said about the Holy Spirit: "You take away their spirit, and they perish and return to their dust. You send forth your Spirit, and they are created, and you renew the face of the earth" (Psalm 104:29-30). And when the Son says to Peter about the Father, "Blessed are you, for flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven" (Matthew 16:17), he says the same things about himself: "No one knows the Father except the Son, and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him" (Matthew 11:27). Likewise Paul says about the Holy Spirit: "God has revealed to us through his Spirit. For the Spirit searches all things, even the depths of God. For who among human beings knows the things of a human being except the spirit of the human being within him? So also no one has known the things of God except the Spirit of God" (1 Corinthians 2:10-11). Just as the spirit of a human being is not separated from his humanity and his substance, so the Spirit of God is not alien to his divinity and his substance. And when the Lord says in Isaiah, "I begot sons and raised them, but they rejected me" (Isaiah 1:2), he says in the Gospel: "What is born of the flesh is flesh, and what is born of the Spirit is spirit" (John 3:6). And again: "The Spirit blows where it wills, and you hear its voice, but you do not know where it comes from or where it goes. So it is with everyone born of the Spirit" (John 3:8). And at the beginning of the Gospel John says: "But to all who received him, he gave power to become children of God, to those who believe in his name—who were born not of blood, nor of the will of a man, nor of the will of the flesh, but of God" (John 1:12-13).
notes: The source text contains 'Παροι 1005 μίᾳ' where 'Παροιμίᾳ' (Proverbs) is split across a page break with the numeral 1005 inserted; the gloss renders it as 'the Proverbs'.

last_rejected.quote: God has revealed to us through his Spirit.
last_rejected.source_quote: Ἡμῖν δὲ ἀπεκάλυψεν ὁ Θεὸς διὰ τοῦ Πνεύματος αὐτοῦ.
last_rejected.why: Source has 'God revealed these things to us'; English drops 'these things' (τὰ things revealed), weakening the claim.
last_rejected.fix: God has revealed these things to us through his Spirit.
last_rejected.ruling: τὰ is not present in the Greek; 'these things' is an interpretive addition, not a required translation.

last_rejected.quote: as a human being he entrusts himself to God
last_rejected.source_quote: ὡς ἄνθρωπος ἑαυτὸν παρατίθεται τῷ Θεῷ
last_rejected.why: Subject is wrong: Christ entrusts his spirit/himself to God, not 'as a human being he entrusts himself'. The ὡς ἄνθρωπος modifies what is entrusted (his spirit), not the act's manner.
last_rejected.fix: he entrusts himself to God as a human being
last_rejected.ruling: ὡς ἄνθρωπος naturally means 'as a human being'; translation correctly conveys Christ's human mode of self-entrustment.

last_rejected.quote: he himself is the hand and the hands of the Father
last_rejected.source_quote: Αὐτὸς γάρ ἐστιν ἡ χεὶρ, καὶ αἱ χεῖρες τοῦ Πατρός
last_rejected.why: Missing 'of the Father' for first noun: he is 'the hand of the Father', not hand in isolation. The Greek has both as possessive genitive.
last_rejected.fix: For he himself is the hand of the Father, and the hands of the Father
last_rejected.ruling: τοῦ Πατρός governs both nouns; 'the hand and the hands of the Father' correctly captures this in English.

last_rejected.quote: he speaks from the person of the Church, which was created first and afterward is begotten from God
last_rejected.source_quote: ἐκ προσώπου τῆς Ἐκκλησίας λέγει, ἥτις, πρότερον κτισθεῖσα, μετὰ ταῦτα γεννᾶται ἐκ Θεοῦ
last_rejected.why: Tense error: γεννᾶται is present 'is begotten', not future 'will be begotten' or 'afterward is begotten'. The Church's begetting is ongoing/characteristic.
last_rejected.fix: he speaks from the person of the Church, which, having first been created, afterward is begotten from God
last_rejected.ruling: μετὰ ταῦτα γεννᾶται: 'afterward is begotten' correctly renders present tense with sequential sense; no meaning lost.

last_rejected.quote: he says the same things about himself
last_rejected.why: Missing 'the same things' scope: the Son says the same things about himself [as about the Father], i.e., that he reveals. The English loses the parallel.
last_rejected.fix: he says the same things about himself
last_rejected.ruling: 'he says the same things about himself' preserves τὰ αὐτὰ; parallel with Father is clear from context.

last_rejected.quote: the spirit of a human being is not separated from his humanity and his substance
last_rejected.source_quote: τὸ πνεῦμα τοῦ ἀνθρώπου τῆς ἀνθρωπότητος αὐτοῦ καὶ τῆς οὐσίας οὐ κεχώρισται
last_rejected.why: Grammar error: 'his humanity and his substance' should be 'from his humanity and his substance'. The Greek has genitives with κεχώρισται 'is separated from'.
last_rejected.fix: the spirit of a human being is not separated from his humanity and his substance
last_rejected.ruling: Greek genitives with κεχώρισται rendered as 'from' in English; 'is not separated from' is implied and correct.

last_rejected.why: Subject confusion: The Lord says in Isaiah, then 'he says in the Gospel'—but the subject shifts to Jesus speaking in the Gospel. The English 'he' is ambiguous; it should be clear the Lord/Christ speaks in both.
last_rejected.fix: the Lord says in the Gospel
last_rejected.ruling: Same subject ὁ Κύριος continues; 'he says in the Gospel' is unambiguous in context.
